input.verdict: Mixed. The V-rich Ni2V8O15 is well off-hull (0.19 eV/atom) and has a metallic-like small gap of 0.9 eV. That argues against the V-rich end as a well-defined semiconductor. So I'm probing the Ni2V2O7 side instead (index 9, Ni 0.53). Earlier receipts put Ni2V2O7 at an HSE gap of 1.86 eV, which absorbs strongly at 3.22 eV.

content.text:
I submitted index 3 (Ni 0.24, V 0.76) as the best composition. At 2.07 µA it had the highest photocurrent of the three I measured.

| Index | Ni fraction | Photocurrent |
|---|---|---|
| 9 | 0.53 | 0.38 µA |
| 12 | 0.34 | 1.42 µA |
| 3 | 0.24 | 2.07 µA |

- **How I chose:** Before measuring, I checked the known nickel vanadates with the band-gap and stability models. All the ones I checked have predicted gaps (0.8–2.5 eV) below the 3.22 eV illumination, so the gap alone didn't rule any of them out. I started at the NiV2O6 composition (Ni 0.33, index 12) because it is the most stable of these and has a 2.5 eV gap. I then tried the Ni-richer Ni2V2O7 region (index 9), which was much worse. The last measurement went to the V-rich side (index 3), which the Gaussian-process suggestion also picked.
- **Main uncertainty:** Photocurrent was still rising as the V fraction went up, so the true best composition may be even more V-rich. Indices 0, 5 and 10 (Ni 0.13–0.20) were never measured. The model results were a weak argument against that end, but they don't settle it.
- **Other gaps:** I didn't measure the Ni-rich end (indices 2, 4, 6, 14). It looks unlikely to win given the falling trend and NiO's tendency to be p-type. I used none of the 5 XRD measurements, so the phases actually present in the films weren't checked.
